name: Acid body wash (AHA/BHA) for pits

lead: Users lather acid washes onto the armpits hoping for fresher-smelling underarms and smoother skin.

AHAs such as glycolic or lactic acid, or BHA (salicylic acid), chemically exfoliate by loosening dead skin cells. Proponents say removing dead skin and lowering surface pH makes life harder for odor-causing bacteria. Acid washes are well known as exfoliants, and no studies of them for underarm odor were found.

paras: Used in the shower in place of or alongside regular body wash on the underarms, a few times a week, and followed by deodorant.
Reported effects are mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA cautions that these products can raise sunburn likelihood.

chain: Acid exfoliates and lowers skin pH
angle.text: Users apply AHA or BHA washes to the armpits on the idea that exfoliation and lower pH make life harder for odor bacteria. The acids are established exfoliants; no studies have looked at underarm odor.

lead: Acid body washes contain alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) such as glycolic or lactic acid, or beta hydroxy acid (BHA, salicylic acid), which chemically exfoliate skin. In looksmaxxing discussions they are applied to the armpits on the theory that lowering skin pH and removing dead skin reduces odor-causing bacteria.
AHAs are used in cosmetics to exfoliate, and the most common effects are mild irritation, redness and flaking.[1] No studies of acid washes for underarm odor were found among the sources reviewed.

paras: AHAs such as glycolic, lactic, mandelic and citric acid are used in cosmetics for chemical exfoliation.[1] BHAs differ structurally in that their functional groups are separated by two carbon atoms.[1]

Proponents say acidic exfoliation reduces the bacteria that produce armpit odor. The body odor article says odor results from bacteria such as Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus breaking down apocrine sweat, and it lists deodorants, antiperspirants and antibacterial washes as treatments without mentioning acid exfoliants.[2]

When used as directed, AHAs are generally considered safe. The FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel consider them safe at low concentrations, at pH above 3.5, with clear safety instructions.[1] The FDA has cautioned that AHAs can increase the likelihood of sunburn, an effect reversible when use stops.[1]
